content: Many countries have implemented a single emergency telephone number, often referred to as the universal emergency number or emergency services number, which allows individuals to contact local emergency services for assistance. This number varies between countries but is typically a three-digit code to ensure it is easy to remember and dial quickly. In some nations, different emergency services (e.g., police, fire, medical) have distinct numbers, often differing only by the last digit. In most regions, emergency numbers are intended strictly for urgent situations. Non-urgent or prank calls to these numbers waste valuable time for dispatchers and emergency responders, potentially endangering lives. False emergency reports are often prosecuted as criminal offenses. For non-urgent inquiries, emergency services usually provide alternative traditional telephone numbers, which are listed in local directories. For example, in England and Wales, the emergency number 999 is used for serious emergencies, while NHS Direct can be reached at 0845 46 47 for non-emergency medical advice. Similarly, in Scotland, NHS 24 is accessible via 0845 4 24 24 24. In North America, the number 311 is often designated for non-life-threatening incidents or minor crimes to prevent overloading the 911 system. Some cities also use 311 as a general contact number for municipal services or to report issues like power outages. The number 112 is the international emergency number for GSM mobile phone networks and is also the standard emergency number across all European Union countries for both mobile and fixed-line phones. However, it may not function on non-GSM networks. To prevent overloading the 112 system, some countries, like Sweden, have implemented automatic call routing to redirect calls to less busy emergency centers when the local center is overwhelmed. This ensures that emergency calls are not queued unnecessarily. The GSM mobile phone standard includes 112 as an emergency number. In countries where 112 is not the standard emergency number, GSM phones typically redirect 112 calls to the local emergency number. This feature is particularly beneficial for foreign travelers who may not know the local emergency number. Most GSM phones can dial 112 even when the keypad is locked, the phone lacks a SIM card, or the PIN has not been entered. Using 112 on a GSM phone can be advantageous because it is universally recognized as an emergency number. Dialing other emergency numbers may fail if the phone cannot roam onto another network, but dialing 112 forces the phone to connect to any available network. However, some GSM networks, particularly in Latin America, do not allow 112 calls without a SIM card or require a SIM card with credit. Emergency numbers on mobile phones can present challenges for operators. Many phones allow emergency numbers to be dialed even when the keypad is locked, leading to accidental calls when phones are carried in pockets or bags. In the UK, a system has been developed to handle silent emergency calls by connecting them to an automated system, freeing up operators to manage genuine emergencies. Emergency telephone numbers are a special case within a country's telephone numbering plan. Historically, calls to emergency numbers were routed over dedicated circuits, but with the advent of electronic exchanges, these calls are now often mixed with regular traffic. However, they may still access circuits unavailable to other traffic. Emergency systems are typically configured to ensure that calls to emergency numbers must be answered, even if the caller abandons the call. Emergency calls may be answered by a telephone operator or an emergency service dispatcher, who determines the nature of the emergency and connects the caller to the appropriate service. Dispatchers are trained to manage calls effectively and may provide urgent advice, such as first aid or CPR instructions, in life-threatening situations. In many parts of the world, emergency services can identify the telephone number from which a call is placed, even for unlisted numbers or those with blocked caller ID. For fixed landline phones, the caller's number is often associated with their address, providing their location. However, for mobile phones and business lines, the address may be a mailing address rather than the caller's actual location. Enhanced systems, such as Enhanced 911, can provide the physical location of mobile phones, and this capability is often mandated by national legislation. Historically, before the advent of dial systems, users would simply pick up the telephone receiver and request emergency services from the operator. In small towns, operators often knew how to reach local doctors, veterinarians, and law enforcement personnel and were responsible for activating fire alarms. With the transition to automatic dial systems, concerns arose about losing the personalized service provided by manual operators. In response, systems were developed to allow users to dial 0 for operator assistance in emergencies, although faster service could be obtained by dialing the full number for specific services. The first emergency number system was introduced in London on June 30, 1937, with the number 999. This system gradually expanded across the UK, becoming universally available by the late 1970s. In North America, the first emergency number system was deployed in Winnipeg, Canada, in 1959, using the number 999. The United States introduced its first 911 system in Alabama in 1968, but widespread adoption did not occur until the 1980s. Canada switched to 911 as its emergency number in 1972. The implementation of 911 in the US was gradual due to challenges such as mismatched telephone service and jurisdictional boundaries and the limitations of older electromechanical switching equipment. These issues were eventually resolved with the development of smart or enhanced 911 systems, which display the caller's number and address and automatically route calls to the correct dispatch center. In France, emergency calls were initially connected manually by operators, even when phone service was closed. In 1929, an automatic system was introduced in Paris, allowing users to dial 18 to reach the fire brigade. The service became widespread in the 1970s. The CEPT recommended the use of 112 in 1972, and the European Union adopted it as a standard on July 29, 1991. It is now a valid emergency number throughout EU countries and many other CEPT countries, often working alongside other emergency numbers. Globally, Iridium Satellite phone subscribers and SOS International users can dial 767 (SOS) for assistance or medical evacuation to the nearest SOS International medical center. However, this number has not yet been implemented in fixed telephony. In Europe, 112 is the most common emergency number, standardized under Directive 2002/22/EC (Universal Service Directive) and supported by GSM mobile phones.
